subject: Accessing variables indirectly in data frames: dlply, lm example

messages.author: 0a86bb0ca38ae4f0
messages.subject: Accessing variables indirectly in data frames: dlply, lm example
parts:
The easiest way to see the question is with an example...


library(plyr)

# define data frame
dfr<-
data.frame(i=rep(letters[1:3],each=5),y1=rnorm(15),y2=rnorm(15),x=rnorm(15))

# First, say I just want to run regression of y1~x for each level of i

#This works
lm2<-function(junk) lm(y1~x, data=dfr) # junk not used
dlply(dfr,.(i),lm2)
# (note: function() lm(y1~x, data=dfr) does not work in dlply)

#This works (but will of course not reference dfr in the o/p)
lm1<-function(y1,x,...) lm(y1~x)
dlply(dfr,.(i),splat(lm1))

#But suppose I want to vary the dependent variable, for example maybe
y1 now,
# maybe y2 later
lm3<-function(resp,x) lm(resp~x, data=dfr)
dlply(dfr,.(i),lm3,resp=y1) # fails: function cannot find y1 in dfr
# (with a different error message with lm3<-function(resp) lm(resp~x,
data=dfr) ...)

# Aside
y3<-rnorm(15)
dlply(dfr,.(i),lm3,resp=y3) # works: function finds y3, in .GlobalEnv
# End of aside


# Solutions of a sort
dlply(dfr,.(i),lm3,resp=dfr$y1) # works, but clunky--need to reference
df2 2x

lm4<-function(respName,x) lm(eval(parse(text=respName))~x, data=dfr)
dlply(dfr,.(i),lm4,respName="y1") # works, but really ugly

# Is there a more elegant way to do this (really not a dlply problem
per se,
# but that is the context in which this appeared)

messages.author: dc06d729e023580a
messages.subject: Re: Accessing variables indirectly in data frames: dlply, lm example
parts:
Hi Joe,

I think the cleanest way is to use substitute to build up the formula:

llply(1:2, function(i) {
yvar <- as.name(paste("y", i, sep = ""))
f <- eval(substitute(y ~ x, list(y = yvar)))
lm(f, data = dfr)
})

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: Accessing variables indirectly in data frames: dlply, lm example
parts:
> In that case, can't you just build up a formula object inside the
> function and then pass it to lm()? Something like
>
> llply(varnames, function(nm) {
>   f <- as.formula(paste(nm, 'x', sep = ' ~ ')

It's a little nicer to do that using substitute instead of parse
because it protects you against a wide class of syntactic problems.

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Accessing variables indirectly in data frames: dlply, lm example
parts:
Hi Hadley:

as.formula() will admit a character string as an argument and convert
it to a formula object. If the input argument(s) to the function are
one or two character strings, I don't see what is the syntactic
problem. If they're not quoted, R interprets them as objects; one
could always add a couple of lines of safety checks to avoid that
problem. Could you elaborate a bit on why you think
eval(substitute(....)) is preferred? My reluctance to use it is that
it doesn't check the validity of the expression to be evaluated.

Dennis

messages.author: dc06d729e023580a
messages.subject: Re: Accessing variables indirectly in data frames: dlply, lm example
parts:
> as.formula() will admit a character string as an argument and convert
> it to a formula object. If the input argument(s) to the function are
> one or two character strings, I don't see what is the syntactic
> problem. If they're not quoted, R interprets them as objects; one
> could always add a couple of lines of safety checks to avoid that
> problem. Could you elaborate a bit on why you think
> eval(substitute(....)) is preferred? My reluctance to use it is that
> it doesn't check  the validity of the expression to be evaluated.

Well, it's a little contrived, but imagine that varnames is c("a - b",
"123", "*2"). Text manipulation will create incorrect formulas, but
the parse-tree substitute manipulations will not. Obviously this is a
pretty unusual case, but it's a general rule of thumb to avoid text
based manipulation of code when you have better tools available.

Hadley

Department of Statistics / Rice University

parts:
What about the bquote function?

> yvar <- quote(q)
> bquote(.(yvar) ~ x)
q ~ x

This is part of base R.

           -s

On Mon, Sep 26, 2011 at 09:40, Hadley Wickham <had...@rice.edu> wrote:
Hi Joe,

I think the cleanest way is to use substitute to build up the formula:

llply(1:2, function(i) {
 yvar <- as.name(paste("y", i, sep = ""))
 f <- eval(substitute(y ~ x, list(y = yvar)))
 lm(f, data = dfr)
})

Hadley

On Wed, Sep 21, 2011 at 9:23 PM, Joe Voelkel <joseph....@gmail.com> wrote:
> The easiest way to see the question is with an example...
>
>
> library(plyr)
>
> # define data frame
> dfr<-
> data.frame(i=rep(letters[1:3],each=5),y1=rnorm(15),y2=rnorm(15),x=rnorm(15))
>
> # First, say I just want to run regression of y1~x for each level of i
>
> #This works
> lm2<-function(junk) lm(y1~x, data=dfr) # junk not used
> dlply(dfr,.(i),lm2)
> # (note: function() lm(y1~x, data=dfr) does not work in dlply)
>
> #This works (but will of course not reference dfr in the o/p)
> lm1<-function(y1,x,...) lm(y1~x)
> dlply(dfr,.(i),splat(lm1))
>
> #But suppose I want to vary the dependent variable, for example maybe
> y1 now,
> #   maybe y2 later
> lm3<-function(resp,x) lm(resp~x, data=dfr)
> dlply(dfr,.(i),lm3,resp=y1) # fails: function cannot find y1 in dfr
> # (with a different error message with lm3<-function(resp) lm(resp~x,
> data=dfr) ...)
>
> # Aside
> y3<-rnorm(15)
> dlply(dfr,.(i),lm3,resp=y3) # works: function finds y3, in .GlobalEnv
> # End of aside
>
>
> # Solutions of a sort
> dlply(dfr,.(i),lm3,resp=dfr$y1) # works, but clunky--need to reference
> df2 2x
>
> lm4<-function(respName,x) lm(eval(parse(text=respName))~x, data=dfr)
> dlply(dfr,.(i),lm4,respName="y1") # works, but really ugly
>
> # Is there a more elegant way to do this (really not a dlply problem
> per se,
> #   but that is the context in which this appeared)
>

>> yvar <- quote(q)

Oh, yeah, that's a nice way too. You do need to eval the result
though (although the modelling functions don't seem to mind)

str(eval(bquote(.(yvar) ~ x)))
str(bquote(.(yvar) ~ x))

Hadley
